question: A 67-year-old patient develops a slowly accumulating pericardial effusion. Which structural property allows the fluid to compress the heart rather than freely expanding outward?
cited_learning_objective: Recall basic facts (to the degree they are presented) about cardiac pathology (cardiomegaly, pericarditis, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, valvular stenosis and insufficiency, angina, myocardial infarction, and fibrillation.

options.rationale: This is the stated mechanical explanation for cardiac compression, but the keyed option uses equivalent wording. It would be correct if selected.
The source does not describe the visceral layer as generating ventricular pressure. This would require an active contractile role not presented.
The cardiac skeleton supports valves and electrically isolates chambers; it does not limit pericardial expansion. This would fit a question about valve support or electrical isolation.

options.text: Elastic arteries prevent chamber wall expansion
options.rationale: Elastic arteries expand during systole and recoil during diastole rather than preventing chamber expansion. This would fit a question about smoothing arterial pressure.
The fibrous pericardium resists distension, so accumulating fluid compresses the cardiac chambers and may progress to tamponade.

question: A 55-year-old patient has loss of parasympathetic input to the primary cardiac pacemaker. Which change is expected based on the normal effect of that input?
cited_learning_objective: Associate stages of the cardiac cycle with the flow of blood through the heart and with the function of the conducting system.

options.text: Reduced firing toward forty beats per minute
options.rationale: A rate of 40-60 per minute characterizes spontaneous atrioventricular nodal firing, not loss of vagal suppression at the primary pacemaker. It would fit dominance by the atrioventricular node.

options.text: Increased firing toward the intrinsic nodal rate
options.rationale: This describes the expected effect of removing vagal tone, but the keyed option states it more directly. It would be correct if selected.

options.text: Complete electrical isolation of both atrial chambers
options.rationale: The cardiac skeleton isolates atria from ventricles, not one atrium from the other. This would require a different structural conduction defect.

options.text: Slower spread through atrial cardiomyocyte gap junctions
options.rationale: The source links vagal tone to reduced sinoatrial firing rather than specifically slowing atrial gap-junction spread. This would require a defect in cardiomyocyte coupling.
Vagal tone normally reduces sinoatrial node firing from its intrinsic 100-110 per minute toward an average heart rate of 60-70; removing that restraint increases firing.

question: A 62-year-old patient has an impaired atrial contribution to ventricular filling but preserved passive blood flow through the atrioventricular valves. Which phase has been selectively lost?
cited_learning_objective: Associate stages of the cardiac cycle with the flow of blood through the heart and with the function of the conducting system.

options.rationale: Atrial systole provides the atrial kick that finishes loading the ventricles after passive filling.
Ventricular systole ejects blood rather than completing ventricular filling. This would be correct if loss of ventricular contraction and outflow were described.
Passive filling is explicitly preserved in the stem. This would be correct if blood no longer moved passively through open atrioventricular valves.
Arterial recoil closes semilunar valves and supports coronary filling, not the atrial kick. This would fit impaired semilunar closure during diastole.
Semilunar opening permits ventricular ejection and does not add the final atrial filling contribution. This would fit impaired ventricular outflow.

question: A 69-year-old patient has a valve abnormality that increases cardiac workload by resisting forward flow rather than permitting backward flow. Which lesion best matches this mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: Recall basic facts (to the degree they are presented) about cardiac pathology (cardiomegaly, pericarditis, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, valvular stenosis and insufficiency, angina, myocardial infarction, and fibrillation.

options.rationale: Mitral insufficiency permits regurgitation because the valve fails to close completely. It would fit backward flow into the left atrium.
Stenosis narrows and stiffens a valve, resisting complete opening and forward ejection; degenerative aortic stenosis is the most common stated valve abnormality.
Tricuspid insufficiency causes backward flow into the right atrium. It would fit incomplete closure rather than resistance to opening.
Mitral prolapse is presented as a common form of insufficiency and therefore causes regurgitation. It would fit failure of complete closure.
Pulmonary insufficiency permits backward flow through an incompletely closed valve. It would fit regurgitation into the right ventricle.
